explorer.tutorContext: Phase plane explorer. Linear mode: z' = A z with A = [a b; c d]; it shows trace T, determinant D, discriminant T^2 - 4D, eigenvalues and real eigenvectors, the classification (saddle if D < 0; node source/sink if T^2 > 4D; spiral source/sink if T^2 < 4D; center if T = 0 and D > 0; degenerate cases on the boundaries), a direction field, eigenvector lines, and trajectories computed by RK4 from points the user clicks (or presets), plus a trace-determinant plane with the parabola T^2 = 4D and the current matrix marked. Nonlinear modes: predator-prey y' = y - yz, z' = yz - z (critical points (0,0) saddle and (1,1) center) and damped pendulum theta' = omega, omega' = -sin(theta) - k omega (critical points (0,0) and (pi,0)); critical points are marked with their Jacobian eigenvalues.

sections.title: Direction fields and isoclines for $y' = f(t, y)$
sections.summary: At every point $(t, y)$ the equation gives a slope $f(t, y)$; small arrows with those slopes form the direction field, and solutions follow the arrows. Isoclines, the curves $f(t, y) = $ constant, carry arrows of equal slope and organise the picture.
goals: Draw arrows of slope $f(t, y)$ and sketch solutions that follow them.
Find steady states as horizontal lines of arrows.
Use isoclines $f(t, y) = m$ to draw the field quickly.

notes.heading: Arrows that show the slope
paragraphs: An equation $dy/dt = f(t, y)$ prescribes the slope of the solution through each point. Draw a short arrow with that slope at many points of the $t,y$ plane: the direction field. A solution curve is tangent to every arrow it passes; you can sketch it without a formula.

For $y' = 2 - y$ the slope depends only on $y$: $2$ on the line $y = 0$, $1$ on $y = 1$, $0$ on $y = 2$ and $-2$ on $y = 4$. All arrows on $y = 2$ are flat, so $y = 2$ is a steady solution, and the solutions $y = 2 + Ce^{-t}$ approach it from above and below.

notes.heading: The logistic picture
paragraphs: For $y' = y - y^2$ the arrows are flat on $y = 0$ and $y = 1$. Between them the slope is positive (largest, $\tfrac14$, at $y = \tfrac12$): the S-curves of Unit 2 rise from $0$ to $1$. Above $1$ the arrows point down towards $1$; below $0$ they point further down, and those solutions fall away to $-\infty$.

notes.heading: Isoclines
paragraphs: When $f$ depends on $t$ too, the curves $f(t, y) = m$ (isoclines) are where every arrow has the same slope $m$. For $y' = 1 + t - y$ the isoclines are the parallel lines $y = 1 + t - m$. The isocline $m = 1$ is $y = t$, and on it the arrows have slope $1$, pointing along the line itself: $y = t$ is a solution. All solutions $y = t + Ce^{-t}$ approach it.

keyIdeas: Arrow slope at $(t, y)$ is $f(t, y)$.
Flat rows of arrows: steady states.
Isocline: $f(t, y) = m$, all arrows of slope $m$.
An isocline whose slope matches its own direction is a solution.

example.title: An isocline that is a solution (authored)
example.problem: For $y' = t - y$, find the isoclines and the one straight-line solution.

steps.text: Isoclines t - y = m are lines of slope 1.
A line of slope 1 is a solution where the arrows also have slope m = 1.

example.answer: The isocline $y = t - 1$ is itself a solution, and every other solution approaches it.

Isoclines f(t, y) = m. y' = 1 + t - y: isoclines y = 1 + t - m; m = 1 gives y = t, a solution; y = t + Ce^(-t).

sections.title: The phase plane $(y, y')$: sources, sinks and saddles
sections.summary: Plot $y'$ against $y$ instead of $y$ against $t$. For $y'' + By' + Cy = 0$ with real roots $s_1, s_2$, the pure solutions travel on the straight lines $y' = s_1y$ and $y' = s_2y$. Two positive roots give a source, two negative roots a sink, opposite signs a saddle.
goals: Draw a solution in the phase plane with axes $y$ and $y'$.
Find the straight-line solutions $y' = s y$ from the roots.
Classify source, sink and saddle by the signs of $s_1, s_2$.

notes.heading: A new picture
paragraphs: A second order equation needs two numbers at each moment, $y$ and $y'$. The phase plane plots the point $(y(t), y'(t))$ as $t$ runs; time is hidden, and the curve is a trajectory.

notes.heading: Example: two positive roots
paragraphs: $y'' - 3y' + 2y = 0$ has $s = 1, 2$, so $y = c_1e^{t} + c_2e^{2t}$ and $y' = c_1e^t + 2c_2e^{2t}$. With $c_2 = 0$ the point moves on the line $y' = y$; with $c_1 = 0$ on $y' = 2y$. With $c_1 = c_2 = 1$ the start is $(2, 3)$; as $t \to -\infty$ the $e^t$ term dominates and the curve leaves the origin along slope $1$; as $t \to +\infty$ the $e^{2t}$ term dominates and it bends to slope $2$. Everything moves away from the origin: a source.

notes.heading: Sink and saddle
paragraphs: Positive damping, $y'' + 3y' + 2y = 0$, has $s = -1, -2$: the same lines with arrows reversed, all trajectories enter the origin. That is a sink, a stable critical point.

$y'' = 4y$ has $s = 2$ and $s = -2$. On the line $y' = -2y$ solutions come in; on $y' = 2y$ they go out. Every other trajectory comes in near the first line and leaves near the second. That is a saddle: unstable, because almost every start eventually leaves.

example.title: A sink from a resting start (authored)
example.problem: Solve $y'' + 3y' + 2y = 0$ with $y(0) = 1$, $y'(0) = 0$, and describe the trajectory.

steps.text: Late times: the slower e^(-t) term dominates.
So the trajectory starts at (1, 0) and enters the origin along y' = -y.

example.answer: A sink: the curve from $(1, 0)$ dips below the axis and comes into the origin tangent to the slow line $y' = -y$.

sections.title: Complex roots: spirals and centers
sections.summary: Roots $s = a \pm i\omega$ make trajectories turn. With $a < 0$ they spiral into the origin (spiral sink), with $a > 0$ out of it (spiral source), and with $a = 0$ they close into ellipses around a center. Six cases cover every $2\times2$ picture.
goals: Draw the center of $y'' + \omega^2y = 0$ as an ellipse.
Draw spirals for $y'' \pm 2y' + 2y = 0$.
List the six cases: source, sink, saddle, spiral source, spiral sink, center.

notes.heading: Center
paragraphs: $y'' + \omega^2y = 0$ gives $y = c_1\cos\omega t + c_2\sin\omega t$ and $y' = -c_1\omega\sin\omega t + c_2\omega\cos\omega t$. The point $(y, y')$ travels around the ellipse $y^2 + (y'/\omega)^2 = c_1^2 + c_2^2$, forever: a center. With $\omega = 1$ it is a circle; with $\omega = 2$ the ellipse is twice as tall as it is wide.

notes.heading: Spirals
paragraphs: $y'' + 2y' + 2y = 0$ has $s = -1 \pm i$, so $y = e^{-t}(c_1\cos t + c_2\sin t)$. The rotation from $\cos t, \sin t$ combined with the shrinking factor $e^{-t}$ gives a spiral into the origin, a spiral sink. With $-2y'$ instead, $s = 1 \pm i$ and the spiral unwinds outward: a spiral source.

notes.heading: Six pictures
paragraphs: Real roots: source (both positive), sink (both negative), saddle (opposite signs). Complex roots $a \pm i\omega$: spiral source ($a > 0$), spiral sink ($a < 0$), center ($a = 0$). Asymptotically stable (every nearby solution approaches the critical point) means sink or spiral sink. A center is stable in the weaker sense: nearby solutions stay nearby but do not approach. It is called neutrally stable.

example.title: How fast a spiral closes in (authored)
example.problem: For $y'' + 2y' + 5y = 0$, classify the origin and find how much the distance shrinks in one turn.

steps.text: Real part -1 < 0: spiral sink. One turn of the angle 2t takes t = pi.
Each turn multiplies the size by e^(a T).

example.answer: A spiral sink; each full turn shrinks the trajectory by the factor $e^{-\pi} \approx 0.04$.

video.label: y and y' trace an ellipse

sections.tutorNotes: Video 29. Complex roots a +- i omega. Center y'' + omega^2 y = 0: ellipse y^2 + (y'/omega)^2 = const. y'' + 2y' + 2y = 0: s = -1 +- i, spiral sink; y'' - 2y' + 2y = 0: s = 1 +- i, spiral source. Six cases: source, sink, saddle, spiral source, spiral sink, center.

sections.title: Systems $y' = Ay$: trace, determinant and stability
sections.summary: A second order equation becomes a first order system with the companion matrix $\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1\\ -C & -B\end{bmatrix}$. For any $2\times2$ matrix, $\lambda^2 - (\text{trace})\lambda + \det = 0$, so the eigenvalues have sum $=$ trace and product $=$ det. The system is asymptotically stable exactly when trace $< 0$ and det $> 0$.
goals: Write $y'' + By' + Cy = 0$ as a system with the companion matrix.
Find eigenvalues from $\lambda^2 - T\lambda + D = 0$ with $T$ = trace, $D$ = det.
Decide stability from the signs of $T$ and $D$.
Place a matrix in the trace-determinant plane.

notes.heading: Companion matrix
paragraphs: Let the vector be $\mathbf{z} = (y, y')$. Then $y' = y'$ and $y'' = -Cy - By'$, which is $\mathbf{z}' = A\mathbf{z}$ with $A = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1\\ -C & -B\end{bmatrix}$. Its eigenvalue equation is $\lambda^2 + B\lambda + C = 0$: the old $s$ is the new $\lambda$. Second order stability was $B > 0$ and $C > 0$.

notes.heading: Any 2 by 2 matrix
paragraphs: Try $\mathbf{z} = e^{\lambda t}\mathbf{x}$: then $A\mathbf{x} = \lambda\mathbf{x}$, and $\det(A - \lambda I) = 0$. For $A = \begin{bmatrix}a & b\\ c & d\end{bmatrix}$ this is $\lambda^2 - (a + d)\lambda + (ad - bc) = 0$. So $\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 = a + d$ (the trace $T$) and $\lambda_1\lambda_2 = ad - bc$ (the determinant $D$). Example: $\begin{bmatrix}2 & 4\\ 4 & 2\end{bmatrix}$ has $T = 4$, $D = -12$, so $\lambda = 6$ and $-2$.

notes.heading: The stability test
paragraphs: Asymptotically stable means every solution goes to $\mathbf{0}$, which happens when both eigenvalues have negative real part. (A center, trace $0$ and det $> 0$, is stable in the weaker sense: solutions stay bounded but keep circling.) If the eigenvalues are real, both are negative exactly when their sum is negative and their product positive. If they are complex, $a \pm i\omega$, the product $a^2 + \omega^2$ is automatically positive and the sum $2a$ is negative exactly when $a < 0$. Either way: asymptotically stable $\Leftrightarrow$ $T < 0$ and $D > 0$.
The trace-determinant plane draws all cases at once: $D < 0$ saddles; above the parabola $T^2 = 4D$ spirals (centers on the $D$ axis); below it nodes (sources for $T > 0$, sinks for $T < 0$).

example.title: Classify a matrix (authored)
example.answer: $T < 0$, $D > 0$, $T^2 > 4D$: a stable node (sink), with straight-line solutions along $(1, -1)$ and $(2, -3)$.

z = e^(lambda t) x, A x = lambda x
A x = lambda x, det(A - lambda I) = 0

sections.tutorNotes: Videos 30 and 33. Companion matrix [0 1; -C -B] for y'' + By' + Cy = 0; eigenvalues solve lambda^2 + B lambda + C = 0. General 2x2: lambda^2 - (a + d) lambda + (ad - bc) = 0, sum = trace, product = det. [2 4; 4 2]: T = 4, D = -12, lambda = 6, -2. Asymptotically stable iff T < 0 and D > 0 (a center, T = 0 and D > 0, is only neutrally stable). D < 0 saddle; T^2 < 4D spiral; T = 0, D > 0 center.

sections.title: Linearization at critical points: the Jacobian
sections.summary: Near a critical point a nonlinear system behaves like its linear part. For one equation the rate is $f'(Y)$; for two equations $y' = f(y, z)$, $z' = g(y, z)$ it is the Jacobian matrix of partial derivatives. Predator-prey $y' = y - yz$, $z' = yz - z$ has a saddle at $(0, 0)$ and a center at $(1, 1)$.
goals: Find critical points by solving $f = g = 0$.
Compute the Jacobian $J = \begin{bmatrix}f_y & f_z\\ g_y & g_z\end{bmatrix}$ at each.
Classify each critical point from $J$.
Apply the method to predator-prey and to a pendulum.

notes.heading: One equation
paragraphs: For $y' = f(y)$ with $f(Y) = 0$, the tangent line gives $f(y) \approx f'(Y)(y - Y)$, so $y - Y \approx Ce^{f'(Y)t}$ (Unit 2). Example $y' = 3y - y^2$: $Y = 0$ with $f' = 3$ (unstable), $Y = 3$ with $f' = -3$ (stable).

notes.heading: Two equations
paragraphs: For $y' = f(y, z)$, $z' = g(y, z)$, a critical point $(Y, Z)$ has $f = g = 0$. Near it, the tangent plane approximations give the linear system $\begin{bmatrix}y - Y\\ z - Z\end{bmatrix}' \approx J\begin{bmatrix}y - Y\\ z - Z\end{bmatrix}$ with the Jacobian $J = \begin{bmatrix}\partial f/\partial y & \partial f/\partial z\\ \partial g/\partial y & \partial g/\partial z\end{bmatrix}$ evaluated at $(Y, Z)$. Then Section 4 applies to $J$.

notes.heading: Predator and prey
paragraphs: Rabbits $y$ grow and are eaten; foxes $z$ die out without rabbits and grow by eating: $y' = y - yz$, $z' = yz - z$. Critical points: $y(1 - z) = 0$ and $z(y - 1) = 0$ give $(0, 0)$ and $(1, 1)$. The Jacobian is $J = \begin{bmatrix}1 - z & -y\\ z & y - 1\end{bmatrix}$.

At $(0, 0)$: $J = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0\\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}$, eigenvalues $1, -1$: a saddle. At $(1, 1)$: $J = \begin{bmatrix}0 & -1\\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}$, eigenvalues $\pm i$: a center for the linearization. The populations cycle around $(1, 1)$. (For a center the linear test alone does not settle the nonlinear behaviour; here a conserved quantity shows the orbits really close.)

keyIdeas: $J = \begin{bmatrix}f_y & f_z\\ g_y & g_z\end{bmatrix}$ at the point.
A linear center is a borderline case for the nonlinear system.

example.title: A damped pendulum (authored)

steps.text: Jacobian: partial derivatives of (omega, -sin theta - omega/2).
Hanging down, theta = 0: T = -1/2, D = 1, T^2 < 4D.

example.answer: The hanging position is a stable spiral; the inverted position is a saddle (unstable).

book.label: Section 3.3: linearization and stability in 2D and 3D

sections.tutorNotes: Videos 31-32. y' = f(y): f(y) ~ f'(Y)(y - Y); 3y - y^2 at 0 (f' = 3, unstable) and 3 (f' = -3, stable). Two equations: Jacobian J = [f_y f_z; g_y g_z] at the critical point. Predator-prey y' = y - yz, z' = yz - z: critical (0,0), (1,1); J = [1 - z, -y; z, y - 1]; (0,0): diag(1, -1) saddle; (1,1): [0 -1; 1 0], eigenvalues +-i, center of the linearization (orbits close; linear test alone is inconclusive for centers).

sections.title: Three dimensions: the tumbling box
sections.summary: A box spinning about its axes obeys $x' = yz$, $y' = -2xz$, $z' = xy$. The six critical points $(\pm1, 0, 0)$, $(0, \pm1, 0)$, $(0, 0, \pm1)$ are spins about the three axes. The Jacobian gives a center about the shortest and longest axes and a saddle about the middle axis: the middle spin tumbles.
goals: Show that $x^2 + y^2 + z^2$ is constant, so solutions stay on a sphere.
Find further conserved quantities such as $2x^2 + y^2$.
Compute the $3\times3$ Jacobian at $(1, 0, 0)$ and $(0, 1, 0)$ and compare.

notes.heading: The equations
paragraphs: Euler's equations for a rigid body, in Strang's simplest form, are $x' = yz$, $y' = -2xz$, $z' = xy$, where $x, y, z$ measure the spin about the three axes of a box (short, middle, long). A spin about one axis alone, such as $(1, 0, 0)$, makes every right side zero: the six points $(\pm1, 0, 0)$, $(0, \pm1, 0)$, $(0, 0, \pm1)$ are critical points (the origin too).

notes.heading: Conserved quantities
paragraphs: Multiply each equation by its variable and add: $xx' + yy' + zz' = xyz - 2xyz + xyz = 0$. So $x^2 + y^2 + z^2$ never changes and the motion stays on a sphere. Similarly $\tfrac{d}{dt}(2x^2 + y^2) = 4xyz - 4xyz = 0$ and $\tfrac{d}{dt}(x^2 - z^2) = 0$. Take a start with $x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 1$, so the motion stays on the unit sphere. Each trajectory lies where the sphere meets a level surface of these quantities: closed loops around $(\pm1,0,0)$ and around $(0,0,\pm1)$. The level curves through $(0,\pm1,0)$ cross there, but no trajectory passes through those points, which are equilibria. Instead, separate branches (separatrices) approach the saddle points as $t \to \pm\infty$, and they divide the loops of one kind from the loops of the other.

notes.heading: Linearization
paragraphs: The Jacobian is $J = \begin{bmatrix}0 & z & y\\ -2z & 0 & -2x\\ y & x & 0\end{bmatrix}$. At $(1, 0, 0)$: $\lambda = 0, \pm i\sqrt2$, a center (neutrally stable): the box spins steadily. At $(0, 1, 0)$: $J = \begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 & 1\\ 0 & 0 & 0\\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}$ with $\lambda = 0, 1, -1$: a saddle. A small error grows like $e^t$, and the box tumbles. Throwing a book (with a rubber band) shows it: clean spins about the long and short axes, a flip about the middle one.

keyIdeas: $x^2 + y^2 + z^2$ is conserved: motion on a sphere.

example.title: Check a conserved quantity (authored)
example.problem: Show that $y^2 + 2z^2$ is constant along solutions, and find the Jacobian eigenvalues at $(0, 0, 1)$.
example.answer: $y^2 + 2z^2$ is conserved; at $(0,0,1)$ the eigenvalues $0, \pm i\sqrt2$ give a neutrally stable spin.

book.label: A special 3 by 3 system: a tumbling box

sections.tutorNotes: Video 34. x' = yz, y' = -2xz, z' = xy. Conserved: x^2 + y^2 + z^2 (sphere), 2x^2 + y^2, y^2 + 2z^2, x^2 - z^2. Critical points (+-1,0,0), (0,+-1,0), (0,0,+-1), origin. J = [0 z y; -2z 0 -2x; y x 0]. At (1,0,0): lambda = 0, +-i sqrt2 (center, stable spin); at (0,0,1): same; at (0,1,0): lambda = 0, 1, -1 (saddle, tumbles).

quiz.question: For $y' = 2 - y$, what is the slope of the direction-field arrows on the line $y = 4$?

choices.why: No. The slope is $f(t, y)$, not $y$.
Right. $f = 2 - 4 = -2$ at every $t$ on that line.
No. That is the slope on $y = 0$.
No. Arrows are flat only on the steady state $y = 2$.

quiz.question: For $y' = 1 + t - y$, which isocline is itself a solution?

choices.why: No. Its arrows are flat but the line rises with slope $1$.
No. The arrows have slope $2$, the line slope $1$.
No. Check $y = t$: $y' = 1 = 1 + t - t$.
Right. On $y = t$ the arrows have slope $1 + t - t = 1$, the line's own slope.

quiz.question: What kind of critical point does $y'' = 9y$ have at the origin of the phase plane?

choices.why: Right. $s = \pm3$: one root positive, one negative.
No. A center needs $y'' = -9y$, with imaginary roots.
No. A sink needs both roots negative.
No. A source needs both roots positive.

quiz.question: For $y'' - 3y' + 2y = 0$, along which lines do the straight-line trajectories run in the $(y, y')$ plane?

choices.why: No. The phase plane has $y$ and $y'$ on its axes, not $t$.
No. The axes are not invariant here.
Right. With only $e^{st}$ present, $y' = sy$; the roots are $1$ and $2$.
No. Those belong to $y'' + 3y' + 2y = 0$.

quiz.question: The roots are $s = 0.3 \pm 2i$. What does the phase-plane picture look like?

choices.why: No. A center needs real part exactly $0$.
No. Saddles have real roots of opposite signs.
Right. Complex roots rotate; the positive real part $0.3$ makes the spiral grow.
No. A sink needs a negative real part.

quiz.question: What is the companion matrix of $y'' + 5y' + 6y = 0$ for $\mathbf{z} = (y, y')$?

choices.why: No. That orders the vector as $(y', y)$.
Right. $y' = y'$ and $y'' = -6y - 5y'$.
No. Moving $5y' + 6y$ to the right side brings minus signs.
No. The first row must say $y' = 0\cdot y + 1\cdot y'$.

quiz.question: Which matrix makes $\mathbf{z}' = A\mathbf{z}$ asymptotically stable (every solution tends to $\mathbf{0}$)?

choices.why: No. Det $= 2 - 3 = -1 < 0$: a saddle.
No. Trace $= 1 > 0$.
No. Trace $0$: a center, neutrally stable, not asymptotically stable.
Right. Trace $-3 < 0$ and det $2 + 3 = 5 > 0$.
Right. Sum $= 4$ (trace), product $= -12$ (det).
No. Those are the diagonal entries, not eigenvalues (the matrix is not triangular).
No. Their sum is $0$, but the trace is $4$.
No. Their product is $12$, but the determinant is $4 - 16 = -12$.

quiz.question: For predator-prey $y' = y - yz$, $z' = yz - z$, what is the Jacobian at $(1, 1)$?

choices.why: No. Check the signs: $\partial f/\partial z = -y = -1$.
Right. $J = \begin{bmatrix}1 - z & -y\\ z & y - 1\end{bmatrix}$ at $y = z = 1$.
No. That is the Jacobian at $(0, 0)$.
No. The diagonal entries $1 - z$ and $y - 1$ vanish at $(1, 1)$.

quiz.question: Why does the box tumble when spun about its middle axis, $(0, 1, 0)$?

choices.text: Because $(0, 1, 0)$ is not a critical point.
choices.why: No. All right sides vanish there.

choices.text: Because the eigenvalues there are $\pm i\sqrt2$.
choices.why: No. Imaginary eigenvalues give a neutral center, not tumbling.

choices.text: The Jacobian there has eigenvalues $0, 1, -1$: a saddle, so small errors grow like $e^t$.
choices.why: Right. About the other two axes the eigenvalues are $0, \pm i\sqrt2$ and the spin stays steady.

choices.text: Because $x^2 + y^2 + z^2$ is not conserved there.
choices.why: No. It is conserved everywhere.
